claim_verdicts.evidence: TIP: "Big-O notation describes how the work grows as the collection size, `n`, grows." and O(n) "means the work grows roughly in proportion to the number of elements". "Roughly in proportion" drops constant factors; keeping only the fastest-growing term is the standard definition the lesson restates.
Complexity table row: "`Dictionary<T>` lookup | O(1) | O(1) - or strictly O(`n`)". The claim ("about the same however many entries") matches the amortized column without overstating the worst case.
Definitional arithmetic: halving n repeatedly reaches 1 after log2(n) steps; doubling n adds exactly one halving. No product behaviour.

NestedLoops.cs l.10-16: outer foreach over orderCustomerIds, inner foreach over customerIds, one == per inner turn, so comparisons = |orders| x |customers|. Run (NestedLoops.cs/Program.cs unchanged HEAD vs stage-0): "slow way: 1000 matches, 1000000 comparisons".

seed.sql header at stage-0: "8 products, 5 customers (one of whom never ordered), 12 orders"; INSERTs list customers 1-5, orders 1-12. 12 x 5 = 60; 1000 x 1000 = 1000000 by the loop structure. Lesson text says only "still finishes quickly", no duration.

List<T>.Sort remarks (net-10.0): "This method uses Array.Sort, which applies the introspective sort" ... "This method is an O(n log n) operation, where n is Count." Compat doc: in ".NET 5 and later versions ... calling OrderBy ... followed by First ... operates with O(N log N) complexity".

TIP defines O(n) as work that "grows roughly in proportion" to n, so 2n and n are both O(n). Remainder is arithmetic: c1*n^2 < c2*n whenever n < c2/c1, so a cheap quadratic body beats an expensive linear one for small n.
Ledgered as opinion and phrased as advice with its reason (reading is cheap, measurement settles constants); no product behaviour asserted beyond claims 10-11.

Program.cs l.19 at stage-0: `["nested-loops"] = Sync(NestedLoops.Run),`. NestedLoops.cs l.29-30: `Enumerable.Range(1, 1_000).ToArray()` for both orders and customers, so every order id matches exactly one customer id.

HashSet<T>(IEnumerable<T>) remarks: "This constructor is an O(n) operation, where n is the number of elements in the collection parameter." List<T>.Contains remarks: "This method performs a linear search; therefore, this method is an O(n) operation, where n is Count."

HashSet<T>.Contains remarks: "This method is an O(1) operation." Table: "HashSet<T>.Add, lookup | O(1) | O(n)" supports the spread condition. Int32.GetHashCode page only says "A 32-bit signed integer hash code", so ran SDK 10 file: i.GetHashCode()==i for 0,1,5,1000,-7,MaxValue -> allEqual=True; Count(x=>{calls++;return set.Contains(x);}) over 1000 -> count=1000 calls=1000.

"With no advance preparation, the system would have to scan the entire test1 table, row by row, to find all matching entries." / "if the system has been instructed to maintain an index on the id column, it can use a more efficient method for locating matching rows. For instance, it might only have to walk a few levels deep into a search tree."

TIP defines O() as how "the work grows as the collection size, n, grows", not elapsed time; it gives no duration. That a set lookup and an int comparison are different-sized steps follows from the lesson claiming no ratio and saying only a measurement compares them.
Arithmetic: n x k with fixed k is a constant multiple of n, hence O(n) under the definition verified in claim 1.
TIP: "O(1), pronounced order one, means the operation takes about the same amount of work no matter how many elements the collection contains." It defines independence from n, not magnitude.

Ran `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- nested-loops` (Program.cs and NestedLoops.cs identical HEAD vs stage-0): "slow way: 1000 matches, 1000000 comparisons" / "fast way: 1000 matches, 1000 lookups". dotnet-run.md `--`: "All arguments after this delimiter are passed to the application run."
Arithmetic on the verified loop structure (claim 4) and one Contains per order (claim 11): 2000 x 2000 = 4,000,000 comparisons vs 1,000,000 (x4); 2000 lookups vs 1000 (x2).

Docs opened this round: refs collections.md, standard/collections/index.md, orderby compat doc, dotnet-run.md; Learn List.Sort, List.Contains, HashSet ctor/Contains, Int32.GetHashCode; PG17 indexes-intro. l.32-33: `$"slow way: {CountKnownCustomersSlowly(orders, customers)} matches, 1000000 comparisons"`; only the match count is interpolated.

issues.text: The paragraph under the code packs the set-building pass, what Count(known.Contains) does, why each lookup costs the same, the hash-code spread condition, the step-size caveat and the database index into one block. I had to read it twice to separate the 'why it is linear' part from the side remarks.
issues.quote: Each of those questions costs about the same as the last, because the hash code tells the set where to look instead of making it compare with every id, as long as the hash codes spread the ids out
issues.fix: Split the paragraph before 'A set lookup and a comparison of two ints are not the same size of step', so the caveat and the index comparison form a second paragraph.

issues.text: 'written into the message from the shapes above' took me two reads. I think it means the sample prints fixed numbers worked out from the loop shapes rather than counting, but 'written into the message' is vague and the printing line is not in the shown block.
issues.quote: The comparison and lookup counts printed next to the number of matches are written into the message from the shapes above; the code does not count them.
issues.fix: Replace 'are written into the message from the shapes above' with 'are fixed numbers in the printed text, worked out from the shapes above'.

issues.text: Summary line 2 says 'nested passes quadratic' flat out, while section 6 taught that a nested pass over a fixed-size collection stays linear. Read alone, the summary line restates the misconception the lesson corrected.
issues.quote: no loop and no search is constant, one pass linear, nested passes quadratic.
issues.fix: Change 'nested passes quadratic' to 'nested passes over growing data quadratic'.

issues.text: Options b, c and d each carry an absolute word ('never', 'exactly one', 'every machine'); a is the only hedge-free, modest statement, so I could pick it by wording alone without recalling what O(1) means.
issues.quote: Doubling the number of entries does not change what the lookup costs.
issues.fix: Remove the absolute word from one distractor, e.g. c: 'It costs one step, so the dictionary compares the key against a single entry and stops.'
